content_metadata.description: A step-by-step tutorial on getting started with the Scratch programming language, showcasing basic concepts, downloading process, interface introduction, and simple programming examples.

qAndA.question: What number was entered in the 'move' function to make the cat move further across the stage?
What function was used to create a pause between each movement and turn of the cat?

qAndA.answer: By clicking on the 'Stage' tab and then importing a background image from the 'Nature' category (demonstrated at 8:23 and 8:29).
qAndA.question: How did the presenter change the stage background from a plain white to a desert scene?
What geometric shape did the cat draw when the 'turn' function was set to 90 degrees?

qAndA.answer: By using the "go to x: y:" function set to (0, 0) and the "point in direction" function set to 90 degrees (demonstrated at 7:27 and 7:40).
qAndA.question: How did the presenter reset the cat to its original position and direction after it moved and turned?

text_to_speech: Hello and welcome to getting started with Scratch. Scratch is a programming language available from the MIT Media Lab. So, what is Scratch? Scratch is a programming language ... but it's specifically designed for education. Consequently, it's easy  to use and it's designed for people of any age or experience level. It is designed to be visual,  colorful, and graphical ... and it uses kind of a Lego® blocks approach ... where you connect different  blocks together to build a program. It's all mostly designed to be fun. So where do you get Scratch? Well Scratch is available from the MIT Media Lab ... and it was actually developed by  a group that has the fun name of the Lifelong Kindergarten Group. You can download it [Scratch] directly  from their website at ... scratch.mit.edu and it's available on a number of different operating  systems including ... Windows, Apple, and Linux. So, to download Scratch ... first open your browser and  point it to scratch.mit.edu ... and click the Download Scratch button. You will then see a form, which you  should fill out and ... by the way, if you're under 13 [years old], DO NOT fill out your email address information ... and then finally click Continue with Scratch Download. This will take you to a new screen where you can ... choose which one of the operating systems you want to use. Just click on the program to download it to your computer. After you download and install Scratch, ... you can start it by double-clicking the  desktop icon ... or by clicking these program from your Start menu. So let's get started. When you first start Scratch this is what you'll see on the screen. So you'll see the little Scratch character ... and Scratch tends to call this a "sprite" although I tend to call it an "actor" ... and the actor works  on a stage--this big white area here. This empty area is where we're going to write a script and ... we create that script using the functions shown on the far left. So we can change how the actor  the actor moves, ... what he looks like ... the sound he makes ... control various functions ... and then there's more  advanced capabilities that I'll talk about later. But let's do something really simple. So let's say that I want the actor to move on the stage. So come over to Motion ... and one of the functions I have here is move ten steps. So what I can do is just click my mouse, ... and drag it over here to my script ... and by default, it says "Move ten steps." But let's say I wanted to move 100 steps. There. I've just written a program. Now the great thing about Scratch is .... you can build things and test  them ... and you don't have to worry about hurting anything. So, if I want to try making my actor move here ... all I have to do to run my program is click on it. And if you notice on the stage, ... my actor moved off the stage so I'm just going to drag them back on here for a second. So, I don't want to move it all the way off the stage ... so let's say that every time it moves 100 steps, ... I want him to turn 90 degrees. So in this case, I'm going to turn clockwise or to the right ... and to make it 90 degrees,  I just change it to "90" ... and there, again, I click on it I can make them move 90 degrees. Now if I wanted to move, and then go to 90 degrees, ... all I have to do is drag this block into this block and see how it  lights up? and it will automatically snap together just like Legos. So every time I click on it, my  little actor moves 100 steps turn 90 degrees ... and again and again. Now instead of having to click to  have them do that every time ... I can control how he does that. So here's my little control features ... and I'm going to grab a block here called Repeat. Now Repeat says how many times I want to do something. So I want him to move and turn four times. Notice there's a space here and in that space ... I'm going to take my existing program ... and I'm going to drag and drop it into here ... and notice how the control box automatically surrounds the function that I created. So now let's watch what  happens when I click on that function. Got to look fast because he moves too quickly. That's probably too fast, so let's make a modification to our program. Now in order to grab this little  piece again I just click and drag. Notice I can just take it right out of there . I'm going to put a little function in here so I'm going to drag this one down ... and what I want the program  to do is, move 100 steps ... and then I want it to wait one second. So again, I'm just going to hook these  together. Now I grab this entire block, put it back on Repeat ... now watch what happens. So, I get a nice little wait [period] in there so I can see what's going on. And, to make things a little more interesting ... I can also add a pen. So, I'm going to say Pen Down and ... now when I run my program look what happens. It creates a little box. Now, if I'm playing around, I might mess things up a little bit ... and that's okay because I can also create a function to make things all nice and neat. So, I can clear my screen. We'll add a little more complexity to that in a second. So let's say that I want to  make something a little more complex. I'm going to keep moving 100 hundred steps. I'm going to take this entire program out for a second ... and I'm going to remove the Wait function. And if I want to delete something, I just right-click the mouse button and hit delete ... and I'm going to put this back  in here ... so we're going to move 100 steps and instead of turning 90 degrees I'm going to do something a little bit different. I'm going to go 105 degrees and I'm going to have them do this,  let's say 5 times. Now watch what happens. So, now he's kind of turned off in a strange direction. I keep running this [program] over and over again it makes a nice little geometric pattern. But now if I hit Clear, the actor stays at the same angle ... and in the strange position that he's in. So let's see if we can't fix that a little bit. Let's go back to Motion ... and one of the things I can do is  say, I want him to go to a specific location on the stage. Now the stage ... the middle of stage ... is at location (0, 0). So, this is the X-direction and it goes from minus about 240 to plus 240 .... and up and down is the Y-direction and again goes from minus but I guess about 180 to plus 180 ... and you can see where that the mouse is pointing at any point in time down there, okay? So I want my actor to return home to location (0, 0) ,,, Yeah, oops! We've got a little line here so I probably want to do my clear  after I do that. And I want the Actor to point in the direction of 90 degrees. So, let's see what happens when I run that and so he's back to normal. So I can run my function as many times as I want ... and always return home. Now I can also clean up my script ... just by again right-clicking on the mouse. clicking Clean Up. and it'll make everything nice and pretty. So again, this is my actor or my sprite  back here is the stage ... and down here it shows you the different actors that are on the stage and the stage. So instead of a boring stage it's all just a plain white field ... what I can do is change the background. So I clicked on stage and again ... I can write a script for that if I want and I will go over here to Backgrounds and ...   I'm going to import a picture from those available inside Scratch. So let's add something from nature ... and let's give it a desert scene. And now I can go back to my sprite, ... go back to my scripts and I can run my little function there ... and again I clean up afterwards. Now you can also change the sprite or add a new one if you like. So, for example, on this one, I can delete this actor and notice it also deletes the scripts, so remember that ... and I can pick a new sprite from a file, so for example, I can ... pick one of the animals so let's say that I really like buffalo. So there we have a buffalo in our on our stage. Now, if it's not something that I like, I  can pick something new so I can actually paint my own sprite if I want. So, you can use all kinds of drawing tools and make your own or you can import a sprite from someplace else in your system. So again, Scratch has a large number of sprites as part of its system. And that's kind of a quick and  dirty introduction to the Scratch developed system. www.prevailing-technology.com Prevailing Over Technology
